problem: Source's technical 'dogmatical belief' (the term he introduced in the earlier chapter) is rendered 'firm belief', which loses the sense of belief accepted on authority; use 'dogmatic'.
replacement: I argued in an earlier chapter that people cannot do without dogmatic belief, and that it is very much to be desired that they hold it. I now add that, of all the kinds of dogmatic belief, the one that seems to me most desirable is dogmatic belief in matters of religion. This follows clearly even if we consider nothing higher than the interests of this world. Hardly any human action, however particular its character, fails to originate in some very general idea that people have formed of God, of his relation to humanity, of the nature of their own souls, and of their duties to their fellow human beings. Nothing can prevent these ideas from being the common source from which everything else flows. People therefore have an immense stake in acquiring fixed ideas of God, of the soul, and of their common duties to their Creator and to one another. For doubt about these first principles would leave all their actions to the impulse of chance, and would condemn them to live, to a certain extent, powerless and undisciplined.

problem: Source says only such minds can sound these truths even with much time and care; candidate says even those minds need much time and care, shifting the force of the qualification.
replacement: This, then, is the subject on which it is most important for each of us to hold fixed ideas. Unhappily, it is also the subject on which it is hardest for each of us, left alone, to settle our opinions by the force of reason alone. Only minds unusually free from the ordinary anxieties of life, minds that are at once penetrating, subtle, and trained in thinking, can sound the depths of these most necessary truths, and then only with much time and care. Indeed, we see that these philosophers are themselves almost always wrapped in uncertainties. At every step the natural light that illuminates their path grows dimmer and less secure. In spite of all their efforts, they have so far discovered only a small number of conflicting ideas, on which the human mind has been tossed about for thousands of years without getting a firmer grip on the truth or even finding anything new in its errors. Studies of this kind are far above the average capacity of people. And even if most of mankind were capable of such pursuits, it is clear that they would still lack the leisure to pursue them. Fixed ideas of God and of human nature are indispensable to the daily conduct of people’s lives, but the conduct of their lives prevents them from acquiring such ideas.

problem: 'dogmatical opinions' rendered 'firm opinions'; keep the term 'dogmatic' consistent with the opening of the chapter.
replacement: I have neither the right nor the intention to examine the supernatural means by which God instills religious belief in the human heart. At this moment I am considering religions from a purely human point of view. My aim is to ask by what means they can most easily keep their hold in the democratic ages we are entering. It has been shown that in times of general education and equality, the human mind accepts dogmatic opinions only with reluctance, and feels the need of them keenly only in spiritual matters. This proves, first, that in such times religions ought to confine themselves within their own bounds more carefully than at any other time. For in seeking to extend their power beyond religious matters, they risk not being believed at all. The circle within which they try to confine the human intellect should therefore be drawn carefully, and beyond its edge the mind should be left entirely free to follow its own guidance. Muhammad claimed to receive from Heaven, and put into the Koran, not only a body of religious doctrines but also political maxims, civil and criminal laws, and theories of science. The Gospel, by contrast, speaks only of the general relations of people to God and to one another, and beyond that it teaches and imposes no article of faith. This alone, besides a thousand other reasons, would be enough to prove that the first of these religions will never long dominate an educated and democratic age, while the second is destined to keep its hold in such an age as in all others.

problem: Ungrammatical, awkward 'he looks for it so everywhere' for 'sought for by him so universally'.
replacement: When the conditions of society are becoming more equal, and each individual becomes more like all the rest, weaker and more insignificant, a habit grows up of no longer noticing citizens in order to consider only the people, and of overlooking individuals in order to think only of their kind. At such times the human mind seeks to take in a multitude of different objects at once, and it constantly strives to link a variety of effects to a single cause. The idea of unity takes such hold of a person, and he seeks it so universally, that if he thinks he has found it, he readily settles down to rest in that belief. Nor is he content with the discovery that there is nothing in the world but a creation and a Creator. Still troubled by this first division of things, he tries to broaden and simplify his conception by including God and the universe in one great whole. Suppose there is a philosophical system that teaches that all things, material and immaterial, visible and invisible, that the world contains are only to be considered as the several parts of one immense Being, which alone stays unchanged amid the continual change and ceaseless transformation of everything that makes it up. We may readily infer that such a system will have secret charms for people living in democracies, even though it destroys the individuality of man, or rather precisely because it destroys that individuality. All their habits of thought prepare them to conceive it and predispose them to adopt it. It naturally attracts and holds their imagination; it feeds the pride of their minds while it soothes their laziness. Among the different systems by which philosophy tries to explain the universe, I believe pantheism to be one of those best fitted to seduce the human mind in democratic ages. All who remain attached to the true greatness of man should struggle against it and unite against it.

problem: 'indefinite' (the chapter's key term, 'indefinite perfectibility') rendered 'unlimited'; keep 'indefinite'.
replacement: When the citizens of a community are classed by rank, profession, or birth, and when everyone is forced to follow whatever career happens to open before him, each person thinks that the utmost limits of human power lie close at hand, and no one seeks any longer to resist the inevitable law of his destiny. It is not that an aristocratic people absolutely denies man’s capacity for self-improvement, but they do not hold it to be indefinite. They conceive of improvement, but not of change. They imagine that the future condition of society may be better, but not essentially different. And while they admit that mankind has made vast strides in improvement and may still have some to make, they fix certain impassable limits for it in advance. Thus they do not presume that they have reached the supreme good or absolute truth (what people or what person was ever foolish enough to imagine that?), but they are convinced that they have pretty nearly reached the degree of greatness and knowledge that our imperfect nature allows. Since nothing moves around them, they are willing to fancy that everything is in its proper place. Then it is that the legislator pretends to lay down eternal laws, that kings and nations will raise only monuments meant to last forever, and that the present generation undertakes to spare future generations the task of regulating their own destinies.

problem: 'indefinite faculty of improvement' rendered 'unlimited capacity'; keep the key term 'indefinite' used in the same paragraph ('indefinite perfectibility').
replacement: As castes disappear and the classes of society draw closer together, as manners, customs, and laws change through the tumultuous contact of people with one another, as new facts arise, as new truths come to light, as ancient opinions fade and others take their place, the image of an ideal perfection, always on the wing, presents itself to the human mind. Continual changes then occur at every moment under everyone’s eyes. The position of some is made worse, and he learns only too well that no people and no individual, however enlightened, can claim to be infallible. The condition of others is improved, and from this he infers that man is endowed with an indefinite capacity for improvement. His setbacks teach him that no one may hope to have found absolute good; his successes spur him to pursue it without end. Thus, always seeking, always falling to rise again, often disappointed but not discouraged, he moves unceasingly toward that immeasurable greatness, so dimly visible at the end of the long road that humanity has yet to travel. It is hard to believe how many facts flow naturally from the philosophical theory of the indefinite perfectibility of man, or how strong an influence it has even on people who live entirely for action and not for thought, and who seem to conform their actions to it without knowing anything about it. I stop an American sailor and ask why the ships of his country are built to last such a short time. He answers without hesitation that the art of navigation is making such rapid progress every day that the finest vessel would become almost useless if it lasted beyond a certain number of years. In these words, which fell by chance and on a particular subject from a man of rough education, I recognize the general and systematic idea on which a great people directs all its affairs.
